The journal seeks manuscripts that critically examine teaching and learning, and publishes original research that contributes to questions in teaching, learning, or teaching and learning. The journal also welcomes novel qualitative, arts-based, non-traditional methodologies. NOTE: All article submissions require double-blinded peer review, which normally takes three to four months to complete. The JTL is published at least twice a year. title: Through the Lens of Pleasure: Joy-Centred Pedagogy Through Somatic and Arts-Based Engagements
text_snippet: Through the Lens of Pleasure: Joy-Centred Pedagogy Through Somatic and Arts-Based Engagements In a time in which the academic world mirrors the challenges and crises of the wider world, we consider and advocate for joy-centred pedagogy. Studying three educational spaces under one departmental umbrella, we connect the sensual and experiential aspects of attuning to joy. We share the ways in which joy is not a destination. Rather, joy emerges in higher educational settings when we share in the practices that are connective and focused. We expound on three examples of joy-centred pedagogy in higher education: a sex-ed learning placement for pre-service teachers taught and experienced through the lens of pleasure and joy; joy/pleasure-centred bubble painting within an arts education research group; and a joy/pleasure-centred education graduate course where bodies push against the edge of AI. Themes such as experiential sensuous learning, care in community, and curiosity serve to help identify what incites joy in teaching and learning.

title: Teaching with Joy: Strategies for Students with Behavioural Difficulties
text_snippet: Teaching with Joy: Strategies for Students with Behavioural Difficulties The current educational context, characterized by increasingly diverse learner profiles, makes classroom behaviour management particularly complex. Teachers face a wide range of challenges, from minor disruptions to more serious behavioural issues, which may negatively affect both classroom climate and the well-being of students and teachers. This study is based on a survey of 76 secondary school teachers from various disciplines who work with students exhibiting behavioural difficulties. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, combining qualitative and quantitative data. The study examines teachers’ classroom management strategies and their contribution to fostering a positive classroom climate, enhancing student engagement and motivation, and supporting emotional well-being and joy in learning. It also explores the effectiveness of teacher training, the challenges encountered, and the need for professional support, resources, and development. Based on the findings, the study proposes recommendations to support the development of an inclusive, joy-centred, and resilient pedagogy that promotes student flourishing and a positive learning environment. title: Play as a Climate-Shifting Pedagogy: Cultivating Joy and Engagement in Higher Education
text_snippet: Play as a Climate-Shifting Pedagogy: Cultivating Joy and Engagement in Higher Education Many faculty report increasing demands within higher education, including larger class sizes, pressure associated with the broader political climate, increasing student distress, and greater difficulty engaging students (APA, 2023; Boamah et al., 2022; Fernández-Suárez et al., 2021; Wiley, 2024). These conditions have been associated with increased stress and burnout among faculty (Boamah et al., 2022; Leiter & Maslach, 2004). These pressures may contribute to a tightening of classroom climates as instructors and students adapt to increasingly constrained learning environments. This article proposes playful pedagogy as one approach for shifting classroom conditions. I present the idea of overlapping climates (i.e., attentional, power and authorship, social and relational, and meaning-making climates) and describe how play can create climate shifts that positively influence how students experience learning and how instructors experience teaching. Tangible examples are given to show how play can loosen overly controlled environments, capture attention, and invite co-construction of meaning. title: Joy as Epistemic Energy: How Emotional–Epistemic Interactions Enhance Scientific Sense-Making, Conceptual Understanding, and Student Agency
text_snippet: Joy as Epistemic Energy: How Emotional–Epistemic Interactions Enhance Scientific Sense-Making, Conceptual Understanding, and Student Agency Amid increasing student disengagement, emotional distress, and performance-driven science instruction, this paper examines joy-centred pedagogy as a critical mechanism for fostering students’ scientific sense-making and agency. Drawing on sociocultural and epistemic perspectives in science education, the study conceptualizes joy not as a peripheral emotional outcome but as an embodied, relational, and renewable epistemic resource that energizes learning. Using a mixed-methods design, data were collected from secondary science classrooms implementing inquiry-based, joy-centred instructional practices. Quantitative analyses examined the relationships among students’ experienced joy, scientific agency, epistemic engagement, and conceptual understanding, while qualitative data illuminated how joy emerged through collaborative inquiry, productive struggle, and engagement with uncertainty. Structural equation modelling revealed that joy significantly predicted students’ agency and epistemic engagement, which in turn mediated conceptual understanding. title: Cultivating Joy Through Making: A Joy-Centred Pedagogical Study of Makerspaces in Primary Education
text_snippet: Cultivating Joy Through Making: A Joy-Centred Pedagogical Study of Makerspaces in Primary Education This study examines how joy is cultivated in a primary school Makerspace through the implementation of joy-centred pedagogy. While innovative learning environments are often assumed to naturally generate positive emotional experiences, limited research has investigated the pedagogical conditions that intentionally foster joyful learning in primary education contexts. Grounded in experiential learning theory, positive psychology, self-determination theory, and maker education, the study adopts a design-based research approach to explore how structured learning experiences can support the emergence of joy during hands-on learning activities. The intervention was conducted in a primary school Makerspace where students engaged in collaborative project-based tasks involving design, experimentation, and iterative problem-solving. Data were collected through student surveys, classroom observations, and reflective artifacts and analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. The findings reveal that joy was cultivated through four interrelated pedagogical conditions: meaningful challenge, collaborative interaction, learner autonomy, and opportunities for creative expression. title: Cultivating Joy Through Inclusion: Teachers’ Practices Supporting Young Learners with Dyslexia in Zimbabwean Mainstream Classrooms
text_snippet: Cultivating Joy Through Inclusion: Teachers’ Practices Supporting Young Learners with Dyslexia in Zimbabwean Mainstream Classrooms Amid persistent resource shortages and exclusionary instructional practices, learners with dyslexia in mainstream classrooms are often portrayed through deficit-focused narratives that emphasise struggle and remediation. This study examines how joy functions as a pedagogical tool within inclusive teaching strategies in Zimbabwean primary schools. The study adopted a qualitative design involving twenty-four (24) primary school teachers from Chivi District, selected through convenience sampling based on their experience teaching learners with dyslexia across Grades 1 to 7. Data were generated through classroom observations and semi-structured interviews, enabling an in-depth exploration of teachers’ practices and perspectives. Findings indicate that teachers can intentionally cultivate joy through relational care, adaptable instruction, and supportive learning environments. Joy was specifically fostered through multimodal teaching approaches, collaborative activities, and the normalisation of learner differences, allowing learners with dyslexia to engage meaningfully and experience success. title: Cultivating Relational Joy: Integrating Self-Determination Theory with Joy-Centred Pedagogical Practice
text_snippet: Cultivating Relational Joy: Integrating Self-Determination Theory with Joy-Centred Pedagogical Practice This conceptual article explores joy as a relational and pedagogical force in higher education, examining its connection to student motivation, well-being, and belonging through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Drawing on SDT’s core psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, the paper argues that joy is best understood not simply as an individual emotional outcome but as an emergent property of learning environments that either support or frustrate these needs. From this perspective, joy arises in inclusive classroom communities shaped by shared learning, mutual care, and collective meaning-making, while its absence may reflect disconnection, constraint, or diminished competence. The paper further argues that cultivating joy-centred pedagogy is not only a matter of effective teaching but also an ethical responsibility, particularly in light of inequitable access to need-supportive educational environments. title: Snippets of Connection: Collaborative Creativity as Joy-Centered Practice
text_snippet: Snippets of Connection: Collaborative Creativity as Joy-Centered Practice This article examines collaborative creativity as a joy-centred practice that faculty can cultivate amid the pressures of academic life. Drawing on our own long-term collaboration as the primary site of inquiry, we define collaborative creativity as a relational, reiterative process through which meaning is co-constructed in response to the shared successes and challenges of faculty life, positioning struggle not as an individual burden but as an occasion for collective invention. Methodologically, we employed social reflection, thematic analysis, and poetry inquiry, with poems crafted from interview data functioning as both analytic tools and affective representations of snippets of connection. Our findings reveal joy as something that arises not through seeking it directly but through doing meaningful work together — and burnout as a systemic phenomenon that collaborative creativity interrupts by turning faculty outward, toward one another and toward the in-between spaces where curiosity and creativity quietly take hold. title: Constructing Collective Joy: Slogans, Social Identity, and Extremism Prevention in Religious Education
text_snippet: Constructing Collective Joy: Slogans, Social Identity, and Extremism Prevention in Religious Education Joy is increasingly recognized as a pedagogical resource that shapes identity, social relations, and psychological resilience. Grounded in the work of Ross Gay, joy is conceptualized not as a denial of hardship but as a relational experience cultivated through care, solidarity, and collective endeavor within educational spaces. However, empirical studies on how collective joy is mediated through organizational symbols—particularly among female students in value-based educational communities—remain scarce. This study examined how female students at Pondok Pesantren Salafiyah Syafi'iyah Situbondo construct their identity through organizational slogans and explored their affective experiences and behavioral orientations in the context of extremism prevention, through a joy-centered pedagogical lens. A phenomenological approach was employed with 40 female student participants selected via purposive and key informant sampling. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and analyzed through phenomenological description, horizontalization, thematic clustering, and essence formulation. title: The Delightful Unessay: How Learners’ Freedom to Choose an Assessment Modality Sparks Pedagogical Joy (Even in the Age of AI)
text_snippet: The Delightful Unessay: How Learners’ Freedom to Choose an Assessment Modality Sparks Pedagogical Joy (Even in the Age of AI) In this article, I argue that one of the principle ways that unessay assignments bring joy to college educators is by creating opportunities for us to work with students who are creatively and meaningfully engaging in our course content—the research fields and disciplinary tools of our own scholarly passions—using an assessment modality of their own choice. After an overview of what an unessay assignment entails, I describe how it facilitates unlearning passivity for students and unlearning didactic teaching and the transmission model of education for faculty. The unessay creates more freedom for learners to explore their own unique ideas and to find personally relevant meaning in an academic subject, making teaching with unessays an intellectually and pedagogically rewarding, even joyful, task for professors—something we all need more of in “the age of AI.”

title: Sharing the Tea: Warming Up the Classroom in Cold Times
text_snippet: Sharing the Tea: Warming Up the Classroom in Cold Times As evidenced by the grim gazes and demeanors of students as they quietly settle into their seats for the day, the Polycrisis, defined as the “…multiple co-occurring, causally entangled crises with synergistic and cascading effects on multiple systems degrading humanity’s prospects…” (Rakowski et al., 2025), is clearly infecting, exacerbating, and curdling the potential of our young people trying to carve their way through an increasingly unstable world. In the face of such iron frost upon the world stage, educators have a genuine opportunity to reinvigorate hope and joy for learning by thawing the perceptual chill with pedagogical practices that enflame warmth and laughter within the classroom. To this end, I will draw on empirical evidence supporting embodied cognition, highlighting the sociocultural interplay between physicality and mental states (Macrine & Fugate, 2022) to illustrate what I call ‘Cozy Pedagogy’. This novel form of classroom community building includes practices such as sharing tea from around the world with students in order to infuse warmth and wellbeing into our classroom dynamics, building new and lasting relationships for collective resilience.

title: Cultivating Joy through Translanguaging Pedagogy: Inclusion and Justice in Multilingual Classrooms in Pakistan
text_snippet: Cultivating Joy through Translanguaging Pedagogy: Inclusion and Justice in Multilingual Classrooms in Pakistan Abstract Using a qualitative multiple-case study design, this study examines how joy-centred translanguaging pedagogy promotes inclusion and justice in multilingual ESL classrooms in Pakistan. Grounded in the framework of translanguaging space, the study draws on classroom observations and semi-structured interviews with 2 teachers and 4 students. The analysis focuses on linguistic belonging, participation, language hierarchies, and student voice. Findings indicate that translanguaging supports identity validation and engagement; however, its effectiveness depends significantly on teachers’ affective and relational practices. Classrooms characterized by empathy, respect, and supportive feedback enabled greater student participation and a stronger sense of belonging. The study concludes that inclusion and justice emerge through the intersection of translanguaging practices and positive classroom relationships, positioning joy as central to equitable multilingual pedagogy.

title: Listening Towards Joy: Journalistic Learning and the Civic Possibilities of Writing Pedagogy in Teacher Education
text_snippet: Listening Towards Joy: Journalistic Learning and the Civic Possibilities of Writing Pedagogy in Teacher Education Academic writing instruction often positions argumentation and persuasion as the primary modes of civic discourse, reinforcing adversarial forms of public discourse beyond the classroom. This article argues that writing pedagogy centred on joy can reimagine civic writing, orienting it toward relational learning, ethical representation, and writing as a way of being (Yagelski, 2009) rather than writing designed “to persuade, to argue, to win” (Neville, 2023, p. 94). Drawing on practitioner inquiry and a world-building civic education framework, this study examined how teacher candidates engaged in journalistic learning as a third space (Gutierrez et al., 1995; Moje et al., 2009) to bridge school and out-of-school literacies. Findings show that listening—requiring participants to suspend assumptions and attend carefully to others—reshaped beliefs and relational habits for teacher candidates. Joy emerged not despite this labour, but because of it, signaling deep engagement and pointing toward more ethical, relational civic futures.

title: Black Male Principals and Joy-Centred Leadership; Finding “Possible Joy” in the Impossible Search for Mattering in K-12 Spaces
text_snippet: Black Male Principals and Joy-Centred Leadership; Finding “Possible Joy” in the Impossible Search for Mattering in K-12 Spaces Black school leaders are exemplars of joy-centered leadership that is needed in schools today. K-12 principals face unprecedented challenges in the post-COVID era. Specifically, Black male principals experience extreme challenges due to deficit framing that has informed hiring and retention practices, promotion, job roles and job-related stress unique to Black male principals. Despite these challenges, the Black principals in this collective case study demonstrated a “possible joy” approach to leadership while experiencing marginal mattering (minimal recognition; insignificance) and partial mattering (selective mattering based on talent/skills) in K-12 spaces. In this article, the author conceptualizes “possible joy” as a confluence of dispositions and characteristics comprised of tenets from Black joy and Black masculine caring. The data analysis revealed themes of “possible joy” through resistance, care for students, and leadership rooted in core values and conviction. Implications for K-12 administrators and educational leadership programs are discussed.

title: Happiness as a Component of Recovering Motivation and Resiliency in Disaster-Prone Philippine Academic Settings
text_snippet: Happiness as a Component of Recovering Motivation and Resiliency in Disaster-Prone Philippine Academic Settings While educational disaster response typically prioritizes infrastructure restoration, there remains a critical deficit in psychosocial interventions that cultivate joy to address recurrent climate trauma. This study investigates the utility of happiness dispositions (joy, humour, satisfaction) as culturally mediated pedagogical resources for recovering academic motivation and resiliency among learners in disaster-prone regions. Using a qualitative exploratory design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 tertiary students selected via purposive sampling in high-risk zones, and analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. Findings reveal that a joyful classroom climate is a vital foundational element. Establishing psychological safety acts as a catalyst, shifting students' neurobiology out of "survival mode" and freeing cognitive resources for learning. Emergent themes indicate culturally grounded humour and teacher relatability function as cognitive scaffolds for emotional anchoring. title: Interdisciplinarity and the Epistemic Conditions of Pedagogical Joy
text_snippet: Interdisciplinarity and the Epistemic Conditions of Pedagogical Joy Joy-centred pedagogy has gained recent traction as educators seek alternatives to cynicism, disengagement, and burnout. Yet much of the existing discourse considers joy as an affective or motivational outcome rather than a condition grounded in epistemology. This paper offers a theoretical analysis of joy-centred pedagogy through a lens of interdisciplinarity in education (Babich, 2020), positioning interdisciplinarity not as a curricular arrangement but as an epistemological orientation that resists the fragmentation and proceduralization of knowledge common in modern educational systems. Drawing on the Systematic Oppression of Knowledge and Epistemology (SOKE), this paper argues that epistemic fragmentation produces forms of alienation that foreclose the emergence of pedagogical joy. In contrast, interdisciplinary ways of knowing reintegrate meaning, agency, and relational understanding, creating conditions under which joy can emerge as an epistemic consequence rather than a pedagogical technique. title: Resonance and Joy: A Pedagogical Relationship
text_snippet: Resonance and Joy: A Pedagogical Relationship The world we currently experience is characterized by acceleration and change. Western ideals of individualistic success, along with surrounding social structures, leads to alienation (Rosa, 2019). The purpose of education is to prepare students for the world they will encounter, but what world? We argue that rather than preparing students for a disconnected world focused on the individual, instead we aim for students to contribute to a changing future with a foundation of resilience, belonging, and connection. Hartmut Rosa (2019) has proposed the concept of resonance as a counterpoint to alienation – as an alert and present willingness to enter dialogue with the world. This view of presence has relevance to pedagogy through joy: joy becomes essential for resilience in an alienating age. This essay explores how Rosa’s concept of resonance can provide a conceptual architecture for a joy-centred pedagogy. Drawing on Ross Gay's work on joy and its interaction with Rosa, we suggest that resonant pedagogical encounters create a reciprocal relationship with joy: an emergent quality of relational, dialogical, and meaningful engagements. title: Patches of Joy: Reimagining Teacher Agency Through Art-Informed Inquiry
text_snippet: Patches of Joy: Reimagining Teacher Agency Through Art-Informed Inquiry Joy-centred pedagogy is often dismissed as an “add-on” to serious teaching; however, in deficit-driven policy climates, educators increasingly describe schooling as scripted, dehumanizing, and joyless. This qualitative study examines how joy can be intentionally cultivated in teacher education as an embodied resource for agency, justice, and sustainability. Situated within narrative a/r/tography, this research draws on arts-informed inquiry in a graduate-level teacher education course in which participants created collage-based “patches and quilts” to render their teaching identities through visual metaphor and written reflection. Analysis of this multimodal corpus revealed four interrelated dimensions of joy as both affect and action: (a) inward renewal through reflective identity work; (b) refusal and navigation amid systemic constraints, including high-stakes testing and prescriptive curricula; (c) justice-oriented commitments, including Black joy and culturally sustaining approaches to language and culture; and (d) enacted pedagogy through practices that centre student voice, belonging, and creative, critical literacies. title: I Stopped Managing Students and Started Facilitating Humans: Recalibrating Teaching in Higher Education
text_snippet: I Stopped Managing Students and Started Facilitating Humans: Recalibrating Teaching in Higher Education This reflective practitioner essay examines joy-centered pedagogy by shifting from classroom management to classroom facilitation in higher education. Drawing on embodied teaching practice, it considers the limitations of management frameworks rooted in K–12 schooling and the need to recalibrate pedagogy when working with emerging and seasoned adult learners. Across academic levels, students struggled with autonomy, accountability, reflection, and instructional follow-through, underscoring that developmental readiness does not automatically align with institutional expectations. Rather than responding with greater structure or tighter control, the essay argues for joy-centered facilitation as a pedagogical stance grounded in care, empathy, agency, and shared responsibility. Within this framework, joy is understood not as ease or positivity, but as an embodied pedagogical resource activated through curiosity, relational trust, and the permission to struggle, fail, and grow. Teaching life skills alongside disciplinary thinking became essential, as did relinquishing performative authority in favor of reciprocal learning. title: The Joy of Authenticity in the College Composition Classroom in the Age of AI
text_snippet: The Joy of Authenticity in the College Composition Classroom in the Age of AI Many conversations about generative AI in the classroom often demonstrate a deficit mindset toward students, with assumptions that AI has led to students never completing their own assignments or having their own creative thoughts. As a university writing instructor, I have found these concerns to be largely unfounded. My students are finding their own authentic voices and producing original work, while using AI as a tool to help them meet learning outcomes in ways that comply with university research ethics. In the era of AI—when assignments, thoughts, and opinions can be easily outsourced to generative AI—it is critical that students understand the importance and value of having their own original thoughts and opinions, and the dangers of outsourcing them to an algorithm. Yet, encouraging students to find and use their own authentic voices through a well-developed curriculum, one that both fosters student self-efficacy and incorporates ethical use of AI, can be a joyful endeavour for an instructor, as it ultimately leads to joy for students. title: AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in the GenAI Era
text_snippet: AI Agents, Joyful Assessment, and Third Space: Rethinking Assessment in the GenAI Era This paper argues that assessment reform in the generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) era should move beyond defensive approaches focused primarily on preventing misconduct or detecting AI use. Synthesizing scholarship on assessment validity, relational and compassionate assessment, third space theory, and AI agents, this conceptual paper proposes joyful assessment as a rigorous and learner-centered framework for assessment design in the GenAI era. Joyful assessment is defined as assessment that is safe, emotionally responsive, empowering, and supportive of student agency. The paper examines how AI agents designed for specific educational purposes can support joyful assessment by creating low-stakes opportunities for practice, feedback, reflection, personalization, and multimodal demonstration of learning. It further argues that when implemented within relational and ethically governed environments AI agents can help mediate third space assessment environments that connect formal curriculum with students’ interests, experiences, and learning needs. title: Civic Joy: Making Space for Joyful Classroom Conversations
text_snippet: Civic Joy: Making Space for Joyful Classroom Conversations Civic joy emerges in classrooms in which students practice mutual recognition and collective meaning-making. It offers an alternative to nihilism and apathy, generating not consensus or sameness but a sense of belonging. Making space for civic joy in political and civic education settings does not require professors to be entertaining or fun, but to allow students to discuss topics of real concern to them in ways that allow them to prioritize their membership in a shared world. Civic joy offers students a taste of being in a democratic community, directly benefiting students and indirectly benefiting democracy.

title: Exploring Joy Through Co-Creation: Reflections on Student-Led Course Design
text_snippet: Exploring Joy Through Co-Creation: Reflections on Student-Led Course Design Joy in higher education is often treated as incidental, yet it can be intentionally cultivated through the design of the learning environment, particularly via student–faculty co-creation. Drawing on a redesigned undergraduate Positive Psychology course, this work examines how involving students as partners in shaping the syllabus, assessments, and participation structures transforms the emotional and intellectual climate of the classroom. Rather than framing joy as entertainment or ease, it is conceptualized as relational and emergent, arising through agency, trust, shared responsibility, and productive struggle. Four key conditions supporting the emergence of joy are identified: consequential voice, shared responsibility, relational trust, and engagement through difficulty. Evidence from both student and instructor reflections illustrates how co-creation shifts learning from compliance to commitment and from isolation to community. While tensions remain, co-creation is presented as a practical and adaptable pedagogical framework. title: From Abstract to Alive: Joy-Centred Professional Development for Teaching Genetics in Secondary Schools
text_snippet: From Abstract to Alive: Joy-Centred Professional Development for Teaching Genetics in Secondary Schools Traditional approaches to teaching genetics in life sciences have often failed to equip teachers with effective strategies for engaging learners with complex and abstract concepts. In contexts marked by teacher burnout, learner disengagement, and persistent conceptual difficulty, there is a growing need for professional development approaches that empower teachers with effective teaching and learning strategies. This article explores joy-centred pedagogy as a suitable approach to professional development of life sciences teachers through a university–school partnership. Guided by Placed-Based Education Theory, the study examines how outdoor, community-based teaching strategies supported teachers’ understanding of genetics and revitalized their pedagogical practice. The professional development initiative involved demonstrations and hands-on learning in a local garden and cattle kraal, where teachers engaged in simulations of genetic crosses using natural materials and observed inherited characteristics in cattle. title: Introducing Joy-Centered Pedagogy: Hope for Hard Times
text_snippet: Introducing Joy-Centered Pedagogy: Hope for Hard Times My call for submissions for this special issue began with the unjoyful: an acknowledgement of global environmental collapse, political polarization, social breakdown, the threat of artificial intelligence eclipsing human thought…students who seem lonelier, more disengaged, dysregulated, and depressed than ever. I proceeded to pose the question: How can educators respond to this moment? I noted one reaction might be to throw our collective hands up in despair and retreat into cynical silence: “there’s nothing we can do; we tried, and we’re tired.” However, I asserted there is another way: joy-centred pedagogy. In his essay collection Inciting Joy, Ross Gay (2022) observed “joy is not separate from pain,” before he queried: “What if joy, instead of refuge or relief from heartbreak, is what effloresces from us when we help each other carry heartbreak?” Inspired by this wisdom, the concept of joy-centred pedagogy emerged during the development of a book I edited, Joy-Centered Pedagogy in Higher Education: Uplifting Teaching and Learning for All (Routledge, 2025). title: Joy for Whom? Joy to What End? The Promise and Peril of Joy-Centred Pedagogy
text_snippet: Joy for Whom? Joy to What End? The Promise and Peril of Joy-Centred Pedagogy In this essay, we trouble the notion of joy in teaching and learning. We trouble it because we do not want to offer another status quo, shiny intervention grounded in hegemonic hierarchy. We trouble it because we want to explore how to co-narrate joy in a way that lets us, our colleagues, and our students realize our “magical” capacity, to borrow Sylvia Wynter’s word. Writing as three educators in a single analytic voice, with first-person narratives in which our standpoints diverge, we ask: joy for whom, to what end, and at what cost? We enter through the debate over generative AI because it reveals how students and educators are often positioned as objects of policy. Drawing on Sara Ahmed, Achille Mbembe, and Lauren Berlant, we examine how institutional calls for joy, if not critically interrogated, can function as affective governance, shifting responsibility for structural conditions onto individuals and their emotional performance. We then read joy through traditions that have long refused to separate it from struggle–Black and abolitionist thought, Chicane and Latina thought, and West and North African Sufi teachings. title: The Applied Studio Model in Higher Music Education: Critical Perspectives and Opportunities
text_snippet: The Applied Studio Model in Higher Music Education: Critical Perspectives and Opportunities The Applied Studio Model in Higher Music Education: Critical Perspectives and Opportunities engages with the dominant one-to-one master-apprentice model in higher music education. The volume contextualises studio teaching in relation to current discussions about learner-centred pedagogy, assessment, pedagogy, professionalism, and the sociocultural dimensions of equity and responsibility. In this book the authors consider the relationality of care, the pedagogy of professionalism, the authority of teaching, the internationalization of student support, the assessment of, for, and as learning, the inclusive access to and structural inequities of sociocultural studio practice innovation, and gender pedagogies in vocal pedagogy. The applied studio is pedagogy, not merely a pedagogical tradition. It is a site of practice that requires the accountability of the institution, and the pedagogy demands an ongoing engagement of scholarly practice. While the majority of the discussions are situated in a Western higher education context, the book offers a research-based and ethically defensible re-imagining of studio teaching in the current landscape of higher music education.

title: Teaching and Learning Statistics: Concept Maps and Patterns that Connect
text_snippet: Teaching and Learning Statistics: Concept Maps and Patterns that Connect For many students in graduate programs of study, an introductory statistics course is often required but can bring anxiety and disconnection, as well as a perception that the discipline is abstract and challenging for students to integrate with their own academic knowledge. To address these concerns, this paper considers an approach to teaching and learning statistics, namely, collaborative concept maps. Drawing upon scholarly literature in statistical education, concept mapping, and complexity theory, this paper argues for a view of statistics classrooms as complex systems that self-organize and emerge through interaction, a diversity of ideas, and shared meaning-making, resulting in “patterns that connect.” To facilitate productive and meaningful connections, small randomized groups of students are invited to collaborate on concept maps as productive pedagogical structures to foster connections among conceptual concepts, the course text, other learning materials, and the learners themselves. To this end, this paper offers a theoretically- and conceptually-informed account of a pedagogical design that illustrates how collaborative concept mapping can function as a generative learn

title: Towards Artifactual Literacies: A Content Analysis of Secondary School History Curricula in Canada
text_snippet: Towards Artifactual Literacies: A Content Analysis of Secondary School History Curricula in Canada The literature recognizes the benefits of teaching with artifacts, but questions about how artifacts might be situated within curricula and with what implications arise. To explore these questions within a settler-colonial context, this study conducted a content analysis of programmatic history curricula in Canada, focusing on teaching the World Wars with artifacts. Informed by an orientation of artifactual literacy and a collaborative research protocol guided by an Indigenous cultural educator, the study found that programmatic curricula call for the use of artifacts but provide a dearth of guidance on how artifacts might be conceptualized or the literacy or pedagogical requirements for making meaning with them. The study recommends that programmatic curricula include teaching and learning with artifacts and do so within a framework that acknowledges artifactual literacies and provides support for the ethical use of artifacts with special attention to responsibilities in a settler-colonial context.

title: AI-Powered Language Teaching: Transforming the Future of TESOL
text_snippet: AI-Powered Language Teaching: Transforming the Future of TESOL This book provides a timely and comprehensive examination of how generative artificial intelligence is reshaping the field of TESOL and second language education. It introduces the core or foundational principles of generative AI as well as critically explores its capacity to transform language teaching, learning, and assessment practices. The early chapters situate these developments within the historical evolution of TESOL theories and methodologies, effectively demonstrating how AI aligns with and extends existing pedagogical approaches. As the discussion progresses, the book offers a detailed analysis of contemporary applications, including AI-driven tools such as virtual tutors, language learning platforms, and automated assessment systems. These are not presented uncritically; rather, they are examined through empirical studies and illustrative case examples that highlight both their pedagogical potential and practical limitations. The author pays particular attention to how educators and institutions can integrate such technologies in ways that are both effective and responsible. Importantly, the work engages with a range of pressing issues, including ethics, privacy, bias,

title: Exploring the Evolution of Personal Learning Environments: A Thematic Review
text_snippet: Exploring the Evolution of Personal Learning Environments: A Thematic Review This manuscript presents a bibliometric analysis of personal learning environments (PLEs) over 25 years, drawing on 494 documents from 318 sources. Three scientometric software programs were used in data analysis: VOSviewer, Bibliometrix, and Publish & Perish. It reveals a steady growth in the field, with an average annual increase of 5.7% in publications and an average document age of 8.9 years, indicating a blend of current and historical research. Spanish universities stood out as leading institutions in PLE research, suggesting Spain's pivotal role in advancing the field, possibly due to funding, policy, or a robust scientific community. Spain ranked first in the frequency of contributions to PLE research, followed by Italy, Portugal, Finland, Switzerland, and France. Two influential publications in e-learning were highlighted: interactive learning environments from the UK and digital education review from Spain. New and fundamental keywords and emerging research areas were identified and categorized into leading clusters and types. This process enhances the understanding of the subject matter and facilitates the exploration of novel avenues for future inquiry. The research fin

title: Risk and Trust: The Lonely Journey of EFL Remote Teachers’ Integration of AI
text_snippet: Risk and Trust: The Lonely Journey of EFL Remote Teachers’ Integration of AI Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into 21st-century education has attracted significant attention, particularly in teaching English as a Foreign Language (EFL) in remote areas. This study explores the integration of risk and trust among EFL teachers in Indonesia as they incorporate AI tools into their teaching practices. Using a qualitative case study approach, the research focuses on two remote EFL teachers in Jambi, Indonesia, with at least four years of experience using AI. The data collection method included semi-structured interviews and teaching artifacts, focusing on AI integration, risk, and trust. This study employed thematic analysis to examine the data and identify the key themes in the perspectives of remote EFL teachers. The findings reveal that AI significantly enhances teaching preparation, streamlining tasks, tailoring learning materials, and analyzing student progress. Trust in AI, influenced by its usability, adaptability, and perceived benefits, plays a pivotal role in its successful adoption. However, notable risks accompany these merits, including over-reliance on AI, which may reduce critical thinking and creativity, as well as privacy and data security

title: Self-Empowerment and Academic Success: CliftonStrengths in Doctor of Physical Therapy Students
text_snippet: Self-Empowerment and Academic Success: CliftonStrengths in Doctor of Physical Therapy Students Leadership is vital in healthcare, improving patient care through quality, safety, and accountability. This study aimed to identify common CliftonStrengths themes among Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) students, to explore correlations with GPA, and to assess students' perceptions of their strengths. A retrospective, mixed-methods study was conducted with 121 DPT students. CliftonStrengths assessments were administered, and quantitative data were analyzed for common strengths and GPA correlations. Qualitative data explored student perceptions. The most common strengths were Restorative, Achiever, Relator, Learner, and Harmony. Command, Context, Maximizer, and Self-assurance were the least common. Relationship-building was the most frequent domain, influencing the least. No significant correlation was found between strengths domains and GPA, though students in the Executing domain had the highest average GPA (3.41) and those in Influencing the lowest (3.04). Findings align with those of other healthcare studies, in which Learner, Relator, and Achiever are common strengths. Qualitative analysis revealed increased self-awareness and empowerment when reflecting on their identified stre

title: Transitions to School: Perspectives and Experiences from Latin America
text_snippet: Transitions to School: Perspectives and Experiences from Latin America The book "Transitions to School: Perspectives and Experiences from Latin America" introduces readers to the importance of understanding educational transitions in this diverse region. In the Latin American context, the transition from early childhood education to primary education is a crucial phase that has a direct impact on the development of Latin children. The book presents diverse perspectives and experiences that reveal the challenges and successes in supporting children through this significant change.

title: Assessing Teaching Competencies in Pre-Service Teachers: Design and Validation of INDUCTEACHING Instrument
text_snippet: Assessing Teaching Competencies in Pre-Service Teachers: Design and Validation of INDUCTEACHING Instrument Induction is a priority action during initial teacher training. This period should include formative training and assessment that allows the student teacher to reflect on their progress and the acquisition of teaching skills. This article presents the design (following a descriptive-inferential method of quantitative approach) and validation of the self-assessment instrument for teaching competencies INDUCTEACHING, developed ad hoc, within the framework of an induction proposal, with the participation of 19 education professionals - nine teachers from five universities who teach teacher training courses for preschool, primary and secondary school teachers and 10 teachers from six public schools - and a pilot test of the tool (in pre and post phases) with the participation of nine teachers in training in the last year of the Primary Education Degree during their training practices. The results demonstrate the tool's content validity and internal consistency and indicate an improvement in perceived mastery of competency between the pre- and post-phases, particularly in the analysis and reflection dimensions. It is observed that induction processes improve professional teaching skills

title: Democracy in the Classroom: 'It’s All About Participation'
text_snippet: Democracy in the Classroom: 'It’s All About Participation' This article investigates teachers’ conceptions of democracy, citizenship, and participation in Norwegian upper secondary vocational education and training (VET). While there is ample research on students’ understanding of democracy, less research has focused on how teachers understand the concept. Democracy and citizenship are among three interdisciplinary topics in Norway’s LK20 curriculum, and participation has a central place in both the curriculum and the Education Act, making this study both timely and important in the Norwegian context. This paper examines how the participating teachers understood the concepts of democracy, citizenship, and participation, their teaching of those concepts, and their classroom instruction. This qualitative study draws upon six semi-structured interviews with teachers working in an upper secondary school, whose principal recruited three female and three male teachers of common-core subjects in vocational study programs. The data were analyzed through meaning compression. The findings suggest that teachers view democracy and citizenship as broad, diffuse concepts, yet the concept of participation contributes to making democracy education more co

title: Critical Dialogue: Navigating Internationalization and Invisible International Students in Canadian Higher Education
text_snippet: Critical Dialogue: Navigating Internationalization and Invisible International Students in Canadian Higher Education This critical dialogue employed critical multiculturalism and critical internationalization as overarching theoretical frameworks and uncovered continuous and on-going struggles for invisible international students and racialized nonnative English-speaking educators in English for Academic Purposes programs in Canadian Higher Education context. Utilizing duo-ethnographic method, the two EAP educators’ dialogues uncover ongoing struggles in English language education in English speaking countries, specifically in Canada including Native and Nonnative English Speaker Dichotomy in English language teaching and learning, Deficit Mindset, Racial Microaggressions, lack of institutional and systemic supports for the invisible international ELL students. We are calling for actions in policy and institutional support for all international students to create truly inclusive teaching and learning environments.

title: Pedagogy of Care Equipped International Post-Secondary Students to Thrive in Times of Post-Pandemic Crisis
text_snippet: Pedagogy of Care Equipped International Post-Secondary Students to Thrive in Times of Post-Pandemic Crisis According to several national indices and post‑pandemic surveys, post‑secondary international students remain at high risk for chronic stress and declining mental health. We therefore proposed a multidisciplinary study to examine the impact of a remote, modular intervention program across three wellness domains: 1) Social, 2) Emotional, and 3) Professional Learning (SEPL). These domains were selected to identify areas in which students might benefit most from targeted support. The SEPL modules were designed to help students: Social (S): learn how to network differently through virtual coffee chats to strengthen socio‑emotional connectedness; Emotional (E): openly share fears and anxieties related to educational uncertainty, work‑related stress, and experiences of discrimination; and Professional Learning (P): invest in personal and professional development, continue job searching, and engage in academic or extracurricular activities to build resilience and support ongoing learning. Survey responses indicated improvements in students’ post‑pandemic distress across these wellness domains, as well as enhanced academic achievement in the associated course following the SEPL interventio

title: In-Service Teaching, Artificial and Digital Technologies, and Teacher Education
text_snippet: In-Service Teaching, Artificial and Digital Technologies, and Teacher Education In this issue, we focus on in-service teaching, artificial and digital technologies, teacher education, and several additional topics. We begin with four articles on in-service education. They investigate the impact of repeated video-based self-reflection on the development of reflective practice among in-service English language teachers, a content analysis of programmatic history curricula in Canada, focusing on teaching the World Wars with artifacts, how teachers understand the concepts of democracy, citizenship, and participation, and how teachers structure classroom instruction, self-assessment and reflection strategy. We then share three articles on artificial and digital technologies. The articles examine the potential synergy between AI and non-AI tools, the integration of risk and trust among EFL teachers as they incorporate AI tools into their teaching practices, and a bibliometric analysis of personal learning environments. Then, we present two articles on teacher education. The articles explore inquiry-based learning in mathematics education through the Canada-China Sister School Network and the development of pre-service teachers’ professional identities in a teacher e

title: Multiethnographic Faculty Perspectives on Navigating Writing Support for Students in Higher Education in the Age of GenAI
text_snippet: Multiethnographic Faculty Perspectives on Navigating Writing Support for Students in Higher Education in the Age of GenAI We are a research collective of nine higher education educators and researchers discussing our perspectives on the impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools on the provision of academic writing support to students in higher education. Using a collaborative multiethnographic approach, we employ a narrative writing style that reflects a dialogic approach to our critical reflections on our personal experiences with GenAI within our unique contexts. Our perspectives are examined through the conceptual lenses of positive psychology (MacIntyre et al., 2016) and emotion labour and feeling rules (Benesch, 2018). The ensuing conversation invites our readers to consider with us three questions related to the impact of GenAI in higher education and on student academic writing: how our provision of writing support has changed, what concerns us about GenAI-mediated writing, and what promising practices are being used to incorporate GenAI tools as support for student writing into our pedagogy.

title: Digital Transformation, Teaching Strategies, Critical Thinking, and Mathematics and Science Education
text_snippet: Digital Transformation, Teaching Strategies, Critical Thinking, and Mathematics and Science Education This issue focuses on digital transformation, teaching strategies, critical thinking, mathematics education, science education, and several additional topics. We begin with four articles on digital transformation. The articles examine Xuexitong for English learning, a component-based model of students' readiness to engage with digital platforms, the use of educational technology to enhance student performance in an English for Academic Purposes course, and the effectiveness of a distance teaching practicum program. Then, we present three articles on teaching strategies. The articles explore feminist pedagogy, the flipped classroom model, integration of humour into the classroom, and teacher effectiveness. We then share three articles on critical thinking. They investigate the Critical Thinking Assessment Scale-Short Form, embedding fiction in case studies within a non-literature course, and critical thinking skills. We continue with three articles on mathematics education. The articles examine integration of digital manipulatives in early childhood mathematics, Indonesia’s Pancasila Learner Profile Strengthening Project, and student achievement. title: Benefits, Obstacles, and Expectations of the Pancasila Learner Profile Strengthening Project (P5): Indonesian Mathematics Teachers’ Perspectives
text_snippet: Benefits, Obstacles, and Expectations of the Pancasila Learner Profile Strengthening Project (P5): Indonesian Mathematics Teachers’ Perspectives The Pancasila Learner Profile Strengthening Project (P5) has changed how Indonesia builds its curriculum: a fixed portion of annual learning hours now goes to character education delivered through co-curricular projects. As teachers are instrumental in determining the enactment of such reforms, this study examines how Indonesian mathematics teachers evaluate P5 after implementing it, asking: (a) What benefits do they associate with P5? (b) What obstacles do they encounter during implementation? and (c) What expectations do they hold for its future? A convergent mixed-methods design was utilized. One hundred mathematics teachers from seven island regions and three school levels answered an open-ended survey. The researchers sorted their responses into categories and quantified them as frequencies, and coded follow-up interviews thematically to explain what each category contained. Data collection ran from October 2024 to January 2025. Teachers attributed P5 benefits to students' experiential learning and character development. However, they reported obstacles of student unpreparedness, scarce resources, inadequate training, and limited time. They also expressed expectations centred

title: Evaluating the Shift: Prospective Teachers' Experiences with Distance Teaching Practicums
text_snippet: Evaluating the Shift: Prospective Teachers' Experiences with Distance Teaching Practicums During the COVID-19 pandemic, traditional on-site teaching practicums transitioned to online formats, raising questions about whether these distance practicums offered equivalent experiences for prospective teachers. This study investigated the perceived efficacy of a distance teaching practicum program among Indonesian prospective English teachers during the pandemic. Specifically, it examined factors influencing these perceptions. Utilizing a qualitative approach, semi-structured interviews were conducted with three purposefully selected participants who had engaged in the distance practicum. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis, with member checking employed to ensure credibility. The findings revealed that the participants viewed the distance practicum as less effective than traditional on-site practicums. Contributing factors included insufficient feedback from mentor teachers, a lack of synchronous meetings, poor communication, and inadequate explanations. To enhance the effectiveness of future distance teaching practicums, these issues must be addressed.

title: Teaching Writing in the Age of the Chatbot: Automation, Disruption, and the Role of the University
text_snippet: Teaching Writing in the Age of the Chatbot: Automation, Disruption, and the Role of the University This paper investigates the challenge posed by Large Language Models (LLMs) to teaching and learning how to write at the post-secondary level, situating LLMs as a form of automation affecting both the labour of educators and the labour-markets our students will enter on graduation. The paper argues that the arrival of the chatbot should spur universities to refocus on process-oriented approaches to writing instruction, which foreground the cognitive labour of writing as a practice of thinking. Understanding what writing is – as a practice rather than a product – is critical to understanding the role we should play as university teachers in relation to LLMs as a form of automation that will displace some, but not all, of the capacities that university-level writing practices are meant to cultivate.

title: How do PhD Students Use Generative AI? Reflections on Practice and Ethics
text_snippet: How do PhD Students Use Generative AI? Reflections on Practice and Ethics Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly moved from novelty to ubiquity, reshaping how doctoral students approach learning, research, and career preparation. Yet while universities and the public often frame debates around undergraduate use, comparatively little attention has been given to PhD students despite their dual role as learners and future scholars. In this paper, we reflect on our experiences as PhD students using GenAI across coursework, qualifying exams, thesis research, teaching, and the job market. Drawing on these experiences, we highlight both the opportunities GenAI provides—for efficiency, conceptual clarity, and skill development—and the ethical challenges it raises, including concerns about academic integrity, cognitive outsourcing, disclosure, and employability beyond academia. Our reflections emphasize that GenAI use is not uniform: it varies with disciplinary context, institutional policies, and students’ levels of development. We argue that GenAI is no longer peripheral to doctoral education but central to its practice, and the challenge ahead is how it can be integrated responsibly to support learning, uphold integrity, and prepare graduates for an evolving academ

title: Trends in Using the Flipped Classroom Model in Higher Education
text_snippet: Trends in Using the Flipped Classroom Model in Higher Education This study offers a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research on the flipped classroom model in higher education from 2014 to 2024 using the Scopus database. By reviewing scholarly articles, conference papers, and reviews, the study identifies key publication trends, influential authors, leading journals, and collaborative networks. The analysis highlights major thematic areas such as technology integration, learner motivation, and instructional design, which have shaped the discourse on flipped classrooms. Findings show a significant increase in research output, reflecting growing interest and recognition of the flipped classroom as an effective pedagogical approach. Geographic analysis reveals dominant contributions from specific regions, indicating both global adoption and localized implementation. These results provide valuable insights for educators and policymakers to support the use and further study of flipped classrooms. Additionally, the review helps identify research gaps and guides future investigations to enhance pedagogical innovation. Overall, the study emphasizes the flipped classroom’s potential to foster active learning and critical thinking, encouraging ong

title: Effectiveness of Combined Teaching Methods to Enhance Mathematical Computation in Daily Life: A Study in the ‘Intelligent Thinking’ Course at Prince of Songkla University
text_snippet: Effectiveness of Combined Teaching Methods to Enhance Mathematical Computation in Daily Life: A Study in the ‘Intelligent Thinking’ Course at Prince of Songkla University This study examines student achievement using different teaching methods, including the flipped classroom, instructor-led exercises, and self-study, and seeks to identify the most effective approach for learning. This study focuses on mathematical calculations in daily life within the course Intelligent Thinking during the second semester of the 2024 academic year. A total of 202 students were randomly selected using simple random sampling, and descriptive statistics and hypothesis testing. The research instruments included an online test and an open-ended opinion questionnaire. The findings revealed that: a) students demonstrated the most significant improvement in calculation skills through instructor-led exercises; b) for complex content, instructor-led exercises proved to be the most effective; and c) approximately 60% of students preferred an integrated approach combining self-study with instructor explanations. Therefore, an integrated approach that incorporates all three methods is recommended to enhance the effectiveness of teaching mathematical calculations in daily life and improve students’ computational skills.

title: Students’ Readiness for Activities in the Information and Educational Environment
text_snippet: Students’ Readiness for Activities in the Information and Educational Environment The article presents a theoretical and empirical study of students’ readiness for activity in the information-and-educational environment (IEE) under the conditions of the digital transformation of higher education. The study's relevance stems from the growing role of digital technologies in academic practice, which requires learners to possess not only technical skills but also motivational, cognitive, and social adaptability. Readiness for activity in the IEE is conceptualized as an integrative construct encompassing motivational, cognitive, technological, socio-communicative components. A component-based model of readiness was developed and empirically tested through a descriptive questionnaire survey of students from Ukrainian higher education institutions. The results indicate a moderate overall level of readiness, accompanied by significant internal imbalances, particularly insufficient development of the technological component alongside a high level of motivational engagement. The study identified a substantial discrepancy between self-assessed readiness and objective indicators of its actual formation. This factor-and-criterion model provides a quantitative diagnostic tool

title: The Call to Teach: New, and Slightly Tarnished Reflections on an Old Idea
text_snippet: The Call to Teach: New, and Slightly Tarnished Reflections on an Old Idea Faculty with two to 35 years as professors were interviewed regarding their experience of being called to their work. I used phenomenology to discover their experiences in the wake of substantial changes to higher education in recent years. Results show that the experience of being called, while still present, is mediated by the increasing administrative demands on faculty, often referred to as managerialism, marketization, and massification. These demands have tarnished academics’ experience when compared to the historically rich path of academic life. Implications of these results suggest a changing experience for participants and the need to compartmentalize and preserve that work, which is meaningful amidst the increasing administrative requirements of the work.

title: Transforming Early Childhood Mathematics Learning with Digital Manipulatives: Advancing Technology-Enhanced Cognitive Justice
text_snippet: Transforming Early Childhood Mathematics Learning with Digital Manipulatives: Advancing Technology-Enhanced Cognitive Justice Transforming early childhood mathematics learning through digital manipulatives can advance technology-enhanced cognitive justice by fostering inclusive, engaging, and equitable experiences. Digital tools such as interactive software, apps, online platforms and games support diverse ways of knowing and enhancing mathematical understanding. However, effective integration is hindered by limited digital access, screen-time management, and teacher preparedness. This study explores (a) how early childhood educators integrate digital manipulatives, (b) the challenges they face, and (c) strategies for effective curriculum incorporation to enhance cognitive justice. Grounded in cognitive justice and constructivist learning theories, this study recognizes diverse epistemologies while promoting active, technology-enhanced learning. Using a hermeneutic phenomenological design, the study collected data from 12 educators sampled through homogeneous purposive sampling via semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and non-participant observations. Findings show teachers use digital manipulatives like YouTube videos and smartboards but struggle with lesson planning and implementation. This hi

title: Translanguaging in Classroom Discourse
text_snippet: Translanguaging in Classroom Discourse The book titled Translanguaging in Classroom Discourse, authored by Kevin W. H. Tai and published in 2026 as part of the Cambridge Elements in Applied Linguistics series, arrives at a timely moment for language education research. As classrooms worldwide grow increasingly multilingual and multicultural, the question of how teachers and students draw on their full communicative repertoire - rather than being confined to a single-named language - has become both theoretically urgent and practically vital. This compact yet substantive volume makes a compelling case that translanguaging is not a pedagogical add-on or a concession to linguistic diversity, but rather an ethical and epistemological imperative for creating equitable learning environments.

title: Validating the Critical Thinking Assessment-Scale Short Form (CTAS-SF) from High School Students’ Perspectives: A Sequential Pilot Testing
text_snippet: Validating the Critical Thinking Assessment-Scale Short Form (CTAS-SF) from High School Students’ Perspectives: A Sequential Pilot Testing Critical thinking is a fundamental educational goal that requires the ability to analyze information and evaluate evidence to make reasoned judgments. However, many existing critical thinking assessment tools face challenges, including lengthy formats that are impractical in real-world educational settings and psychometric issues such as limited reliability and unclear validity. This study addresses this gap by validating the Critical Thinking Assessment Scale-Short Form (CTAS-SF) within the under-explored context of Arabic-medium schools in Brunei. By employing a mixed-methods design, the study incorporated cognitive think-aloud interviews (n = 10) and a cross-sectional survey (n = 248). Through EFA and CFA analyses, the study revealed a robust five-factor model that demonstrates strong internal reliability, aligning with contemporary conceptualizations of critical thinking. Evidence of convergent and discriminant validity further supports the instrument's robustness. The study concludes that the new five-factor model is a valid and reliable tool for assessing high school students’ critical thinking, offering practitioners and researchers an efficient measure suitable for classroo

title: Leadership for Building a Shared Purpose of Improvement
text_snippet: Leadership for Building a Shared Purpose of Improvement This study analyzes how a school management team is creating a school that is transitioning toward a Professional Learning Community (PLC). Using a qualitative methodology, the research adopts a case study approach and conducts semi-structured interviews with various members of the educational community. The study used holistic content analysis to interpret the gathered information. The primary findings reveal a shared purpose within the management team that extends to the broader educational community. Emphasis is placed on collaborative efforts, ongoing training, mutual support between management and teaching staff, and the cultivation of intermediate leadership and student involvement. The institution prioritizes giving families a voice and remains open to input from the community and professionals proposing educational enhancements. In conclusion, the study asserts that a clearly defined shared objective, a culture of trust, intermediate leadership, and collaboration are key to establishing a PLC.

title: Ethnoscience and Scientific–Digital Literacies: A Bibliometric Mapping of Global Research Trends in Science Education (2014–2024)
text_snippet: Ethnoscience and Scientific–Digital Literacies: A Bibliometric Mapping of Global Research Trends in Science Education (2014–2024) Over the past ten years, interest in using ethnoscience approaches in science education has continued to grow, particularly as a learning method relevant to local cultural contexts and capable of supporting the strengthening of scientific and digital literacy. However, research in this field remains scattered across various themes and regions without a comprehensive mapping, necessitating a thorough review to describe the direction and development of research globally. This study aims to conduct a bibliometric analysis of publications related to ethnoscience in science education between 2014 and 2024, focusing on publication trends, dominant themes, key contributors, and collaboration patterns that support the development of scientific and digital literacy based on local culture. A total of 104 documents were analyzed after being filtered from the Scopus database using the keywords “ethnoscience,” “education,” and “learning,” with restrictions on publication year and English language. The data were analyzed using VOSviewer software for keyword mapping and author collaboration networks, supplemented by frequency and field distribution analysis. title: Perceived Ease of Use and Behavioural Intention in Xuexitong-Assisted English Learning: The Mediating Role of Perceived Enjoyment Among Vocational Agriculture Students
text_snippet: Perceived Ease of Use and Behavioural Intention in Xuexitong-Assisted English Learning: The Mediating Role of Perceived Enjoyment Among Vocational Agriculture Students Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model with its hedonic extension, this study investigates whether perceived enjoyment mediates the relationship between perceived ease of use and behavioural intention to use Xuexitong for English learning among Chinese agricultural vocational students. A cross-sectional survey of 92 agriculture major students was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling with bias-corrected bootstrapping. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity, and the structural model explained 47.8% of the variance in behavioural intention. Perceived ease of use significantly predicted both perceived enjoyment (β = 0.636, p

title: Does Asynchronous Learning in English for Academic Purposes Enhance Academic Performance? Evidence from University-Wide GPA Outcomes
text_snippet: Does Asynchronous Learning in English for Academic Purposes Enhance Academic Performance? Evidence from University-Wide GPA Outcomes This study investigates how educational technology through an asynchronous online EAP course can enhance student performance at a university in Singapore. Leveraging a quasi-experimental approach, institutional data from 2017 to 2020 were analyzed to compare semester grade point averages (SGPA) between students who completed the EAP course and those exempted based on a standardized English proficiency cutoff. The findings reveal that students who undertook the asynchronous EAP course achieved modest but statistically significant gains in SGPA. These results suggest that technology-enhanced, self-paced learning environments can enhance academic achievement. By challenging assumptions that privilege face-to-face instruction, the study supports the value of educational technology in academic English development and highlights the potential of asynchronous EAP courses as scalable, sustainable, and impactful academic support in higher education.

title: Bringing Laughter to EFL Classrooms: Learners’ Perspectives on Humour as an Educational Tool
text_snippet: Bringing Laughter to EFL Classrooms: Learners’ Perspectives on Humour as an Educational Tool Amid global transformations across various aspects of life, the education landscape has undergone profound and ongoing change in the 21st century. One such change is the emphasis on learners’ well-being, which has received as much attention as their academic performance. In response, researchers and educators have shown growing interest in integrating humour into language classrooms. Humour has been recognized as a valuable pedagogical tool that can significantly benefit both students’ well-being and learning outcomes. However, this topic remains controversial, especially in Asian EFL contexts. This paper explores the potential effects of humour in Vietnamese EFL classrooms from students' perspectives. The study employed a mixed-methods approach, comprising a survey of 207 undergraduates and in-depth interviews with 10 students. The findings revealed that humour offers various benefits and drawbacks for learners across psychological, social, and instructional domains. The study also provides pedagogical insights into the use of humour in contemporary Vietnamese EFL classrooms.

title: Augmented Reality Learning Integrated with Cognitive Conflict and STEM: Impact on Students’ Scientific Literacy in Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation
text_snippet: Augmented Reality Learning Integrated with Cognitive Conflict and STEM: Impact on Students’ Scientific Literacy in Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation Integrating technology with innovative learning plays a crucial role in equipping students with scientific literacy. This research investigated the impact of augmented reality (AR) learning integrated with cognitive conflict (CC) and science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) on students’ scientific literacy using Newton’s universal law of gravitation as the learning material. This research involved 33 upper-secondary students divided into two groups using a quasi-experimental method: one group implemented AR, and the other used traditional learning. The research data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon test (W), Mann-Whitney test (U), and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) analysis. The results of the W test revealed that both traditional learning and learning via AR have a positive impact on enhancing students’ scientific literacy. However, the U test results indicate that learning via AR was more effective than traditional learning. In addition, the results of the SEM analysis revealed that the enhancement of scientific literacy was influenced by AR technological characteristics, self-efficacy, and intention to use, which directly affected students’ scientific literac

title: Validating the Teacher Effectiveness Scale: A Psychometric Analysis of Its Validity and Reliability
text_snippet: Validating the Teacher Effectiveness Scale: A Psychometric Analysis of Its Validity and Reliability This study validated the Teacher Effectiveness Scale (TES) by analyzing its psychometric qualities using Item Response Theory (IRT) and Classical Test Theory (CTT). The TES assesses six components of teacher effectiveness: teacher personality, classroom organization and management, lesson planning, lesson implementation, student progress monitoring, and professional development. A cross-sectional survey design was employed across Oyo, Osun, and Ondo States in Nigeria. In the pilot phase, 40 teachers from four junior secondary schools in Oyo State participated. The second phase, which focused on construct validation, involved 320 senior secondary school teachers from 16 public and private schools in Osun State, using stratified sampling. In the final phase, 240 teachers from 16 schools in Ondo State were assessed for consistency and applicability. Confirmatory full-information factor analysis confirmed the TES’s structural validity with strong factor loadings (0.58–0.84). Convergent and discriminant validity were established for five factors, but Factor 6 was eliminated. IRT reliability analysis showed internal consistency (0.7–0.9). title: Students’ Discomfort Triggers Increased Awareness of Systemic Racism in a Forensic Science Class
text_snippet: Students’ Discomfort Triggers Increased Awareness of Systemic Racism in a Forensic Science Class The foundational argument for requiring diversity or race and racism courses in higher education is that they increase student awareness and empathy for people of other races. Researchers have examined this primarily through surveys of student attitudes. To understand the impacts of courses addressing racism—particularly whether they improve students’ understanding of systemic racism and empathy for people from other races—we need to examine students’ thinking as reflected in their work during the class. This has been done in low-enrolment courses, but the impacts of high-enrolment courses are less understood. Using a theoretical framing based on Boler’s Pedagogy of Discomfort and Dewsbury and colleagues' description of the cyclical journey of growing development of faculty racial awareness, we analyzed students’ written reflections to evaluate their personal responses to a high-enrolment course exploring the impact of systemic racism on the criminal legal system. Our findings support the hypothesis that self-awareness rising through discomfort can lead to desire for personal change in attitudes towards race and racism.

title: Honing the Critical Imagination: The Use of Fiction as Case Study to Develop Critical Thinking Skills
text_snippet: Honing the Critical Imagination: The Use of Fiction as Case Study to Develop Critical Thinking Skills This paper presents the pedagogical approach of embedding fiction as case studies within a non-literature course to foster deep learning of subject content and build critical thinking skills. We did this in a postgraduate leadership course, pairing literary works of fiction, such as Sophocles’s Antigone, with academic leadership theory. Although research discusses the value of literature as a teaching tool, few examples show literary works integrated into curricula. We share our experience and observations, along with an original critical-thinking model, to reflect and evaluate how ideas from fictional texts were applied to students’ real-world thinking. By presenting this subject design and our key takeaways on student learning outcomes, we hope to offer other educators a way to craft their own subject design to engage, challenge, and enrich students’ learning experiences.

title: The Effectiveness of Guided Inquiry Integrated with Local Wisdom in Enhancing Critical Thinking, Problem-Solving Skills, and Environmental Awareness: A Systematic Literature Review
text_snippet: The Effectiveness of Guided Inquiry Integrated with Local Wisdom in Enhancing Critical Thinking, Problem-Solving Skills, and Environmental Awareness: A Systematic Literature Review Increasing critical thinking skills, problem-solving, and environmental awareness are the main goals of modern education, especially in Natural Sciences (Science) based learning. Through a systematic literature review, this research analyzes the effectiveness of guided inquiry integrated with local wisdom in improving these three aspects through a systematic literature review. Data was obtained from 517 articles identified through various Scopus databases and registers, then selected using the PRISMA diagram to leave 102 articles that met the inclusion criteria. Inclusion criteria include articles that discuss the application of guided inquiry with the integration of local wisdom, written in English, available in open access, and published within a specific time frame. The results of the analysis show that guided inquiry integrated with local wisdom is effective in creating contextual learning experiences that are relevant to students' lives. This approach improves critical thinking and problem-solving skills, strengthening environmental awareness by introducing local values.
